proposals.relationship: In their joint Introduction, Jones and Porter credit Foucault’s defamiliarization of apparently natural historical categories and his questions about medical power with productive changes in historical research.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint1994 assessment, not an unqualified endorsement or solely Porter’s wording.4–5 combine conceptual appreciation with empirical objections;1985 own139 also calls Foucault’s biomedical studies stimulating and cites English Birth of the Clinic1973 and Discipline and Punish1977. No claim to fresh reading of those originals.

proposals.relationship: Porter challenges the applicability of Foucault’s great confinement to Britain, where state intervention in madness was less systematic than the French model suggests.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint Introduction4 specifically identifies Roy’s argument and distinguishes Jones’s French qualification and Midelfort/Scull’s objections. Not a wholesale rejection of Foucault. Preview13/n12 preserves Gordon’s warning about the abridged English text; no fresh full French original or Porter1990 article reading. Jordanova2012 memoir507 corroborates empirical and discontinuity concerns, but this arrow is bounded to the directly available British-confinement passage.

proposals.relationship: Porter treats Ariès’s histories of childhood and death as stimulating resources for studying biomedical beliefs within the wider history of life and values.
proposals.evidence_note: Own139 explicitly praises Ariès alongside Foucault while distinguishing both from formal Annales membership. Note9 cites Centuries of Childhood London1962 and The Hour of Our Death London1981; these English editions, not unread French originals, identify the resource. This is a scoped methodological resource, not an assertion that all Ariès’s claims were accepted.

proposals.relationship: Porter uses Burke’s analysis of popular culture to question rigid separations between lay and elite medical cultures.
proposals.evidence_note: Own163/n147 explicitly directs readers to Burke on shortcomings of two-culture stratification models as Porter argues lay culture overlapped professional medicine. Note147 continues164 and shares credit with Payne, Muchembled and methodological discussions; no claim Burke alone originated Porter’s argument. Earlier140/n11 also frames the cultural-strata problem. Cited originals unread here.

proposals.relationship: Bacopoulos-Viau and Fauvel interpret Porter’s patient history as an adaptation of Thompson’s history from below and agency, quoting Porter’s recollection that The Making changed how he saw historical writing.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed2016 scholarly mediation:4/n20 identifies a1997 Lancet interview, not independently read here, and explains the conceptual adaptation from working-class subjectivity to sufferers’ experience. No direct mentorship or proven first-reading date. Porter’s own163/n146 cites Thompson among recreation/culture analogies, but does not alone demonstrate the whole formative claim.

proposals.relationship: Porter credits Annales historians’ reconstruction of material life, beliefs and behaviour as a major resource for his wider social history of lay health and sickness.
proposals.evidence_note: Own139 expressly describes Annales as pioneering these perspectives and explains why material life requires medical beliefs and behaviour; note7 names French medical historians and1975/1980 translated collections. Group-level acknowledged approach, not an inferred personal relation to every Annaliste; Foucault and Ariès explicitly stand outside the formal fold.
